sections.h2: Which Louisville offices value and bill your house
sections.html:
The PVA values your house, and the Sheriff bills it. The Sheriff's office gathers about $1 billion a year from over 300,000 taxpayers for 13 taxing jurisdictions, among them the state, Louisville Metro, the school board and several fire districts.

The PVA is in the Glassworks Building, 815 W. Market St., Suite 400, Louisville, KY 40202, phone (502) 574-6380. The Sheriff's Property Tax Department is inside the Fiscal Court Building at 700 W. Liberty St., phone (502) 574-5479, and takes walk-in payers from 8 AM until 4 PM on business days.

The PVA measures fair cash value as of each January 1. Whoever the records name as owner on that date, or when the roll is printed, receives the bill.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
Bills are due out by November 1. The 2 percent early-pay discount lasts until December 1, and then the stages step up on the Sheriff's calendar.

Payment stages for the current-year Jefferson County tax bill
DatesAmount owed
November 1 to December 1Bill less 2 percent
December 2 to January 4Bill at face value
January 5 to February 5Face value plus 5 percent
February 6 to April 15Face value plus a 10 percent penalty and a 10 percent Sheriff's add-on fee

When the last day of a stage lands on a Saturday, Sunday or office holiday, it rolls forward to the next open day. A missing bill still carries the late charges, so call the department if yours hasn't come.

  • In person: cash, check or money order, with the stub from your bill.
  • Mail: make the check out to Jefferson County Sheriff and send it to PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570.
  • Web portal: eChecks run $2, and cards run 2.25 percent, or a flat $1.95 when the payment is $86 or less.
  • Dropboxes sit at the downtown office and at County Clerk branches such as Dixie, Fairdale, Highview, East and Westport.

Installment-style payments toward a current bill are also taken between November 1 and April 15.

sections.h2: How to challenge a PVA valuation
sections.html:
The route starts with a PVA conference, not a board hearing. KRS 133.120 sets that order, the conference falls in the yearly open inspection period, and Jefferson County runs it through an online form.

  • File one conference per parcel ID.
  • Attach an appraisal, photographs, an insurance policy, repair quotes, construction costs or a listing agreement.
  • Pick comparable sales from about the last two years, matched on size and type. The PVA opens its sales search to the public free for the appeal window.
  • Results come back in writing within roughly one to two weeks.

If the conference result stands, complete the lower section of that form and deliver it to the Jefferson County Clerk. State law sets the filing deadline at one workday after the inspection period ends. The Local Board of Assessment Appeals hears the case, and skipping that board forecloses the Board of Tax Appeals. Paid representatives need written authorization and must fit a listed profession.

An appeal never pauses collection. Pay tax on your own claimed figure now. A higher number from the board brings a supplemental bill with interest.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption and West End help
sections.html:
The figure for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years is $49,100, subtracted from an eligible home's assessment. Eligible means 65 or older, or totally disabled, and living in the house.

The deduction shrinks a bill but never erases it unless the assessment is smaller than the deduction. Bring proof of age to the PVA, such as a passport, birth certificate or license. Disability claims need proof of benefits from a federal or retirement-system program.

West End homeowners may have another option. LHOME and the West End Opportunity Partnership offer a grant or 0 percent loan toward the residential bill in nine neighborhoods: Algonquin, California, Chickasaw, Park DuValle, Parkhill, Parkland, Portland, Russell and Shawnee. LHOME's number is (502) 882-8091.

sections.h2: City taxes on top of the Sheriff's bill
sections.html:
Often there are. The Sheriff's bill funds the state, Metro, schools and fire districts, while many smaller cities inside the county bill their own residents on top.

The PVA tallies 83 incorporated taxing jurisdictions among roughly 60,000 properties. Those cities offer services such as police, sanitation and parks, with rates posted by each city. State law has recognized just two city classes since 2015: first class, which is Louisville, and home rule cities, which are all the rest.

A seller in a place like St. Matthews or Jeffersontown should call city hall for a balance and a payoff letter. Looking only at the Sheriff's account can miss a separate city liability.

The debt sticks to the owner and the land alike. KRS 134.015 calls it the taxpayer's personal obligation from the assessment date, and the KRS 134.420 lien can run 11 years no matter who holds title.

Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the Clerk, where monthly interest of 1 percent and extra fees start. An outside investor may buy the certificate at the summer sale, and the County Attorney's page estimates the added cost near 40 percent.

A County Attorney payment plan keeps a bill out of that sale, though plans for a given year open only after the Sheriff's collection period closes. Requests to waive certain penalties go in writing to the same office.

The usual closing split is that the seller pays a prorated share for the months owned, and the buyer settles the whole bill when it arrives. Read your settlement statement to see how the closing agent divided it. Closing doesn't wipe out a lien, so the title company will clear it from your proceeds. Get a current-year figure from the Sheriff and earlier-year figures from the Clerk.

Kentucky's most populous county counted 795,222 people in the 2025 estimate, inside borders it shares with Louisville Metro. Land area is 380.8 square miles.

  • Owned homes had a middle value of $248,400.
  • Owners live in 62.1 percent of homes.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,593 with a mortgage and $608 without.
  • Median household income: $69,866.
  • Housing units in 2025: 366,702.

Children attend Jefferson County Public Schools, or the Anchorage Independent district through eighth grade. Deed recording questions go to the County Clerk's Legal Records Division.

Call the Sheriff for the current-year balance and the Clerk for anything older, and ask city hall about a separate city bill if your house is in one of the smaller cities. Put all the figures in writing so the title company can pay them from your proceeds.

If you think the PVA's number is too high, act during the inspection period, because a tax bill arrives too late to contest. Start with the online conference and use the Clerk petition only if the conference fails. A cash sale doesn't skip any of this, since liens and city balances still have to be cleared before the deed passes.

faqs.q: Where can I hand in a Jefferson County tax payment?
faqs.a: Walk-in payments are taken downtown at 700 W. Liberty St. between 8 AM and 4 PM Monday to Friday, cash, checks and money orders only. You can also pay online, drop an envelope in a dropbox or mail PO Box 34570.

faqs.q: How long does the 2 percent early discount last?
faqs.a: The 2 percent discount covers payments received between November 1 and December 1 inclusive. Face value applies until January 4, and a 5 percent charge starts January 5.

faqs.q: Will the Sheriff take part of a bill now and the rest later?
faqs.a: Yes. Part payments on a current-year bill are accepted while collection runs, and once the bill moves to the Clerk the County Attorney decides who qualifies for a plan.

faqs.q: How early must I act to lower my assessment?
faqs.a: Act during the yearly inspection period, because a tax bill arrives too late to contest. File the PVA's online conference first. Only a failed conference opens the door to a petition at the Clerk.

faqs.q: Does closing on the sale wipe out a tax lien?
faqs.a: No. A lien outlives a sale, and the title company will insist on clearing it out of your proceeds. Obtain a current-year figure from the Sheriff and earlier-year figures from the Clerk.
